attributes.clauseText:
The product's functions are those specified by the manufacturer and provided when the product is used
according to its IPRFU.
NOTE      The Remote Data Processing Solutions (RDPS) interfaces and dependencies are part of the product
functions.
EXAMPLE 1 The functions of a product that are remotely executed or are needed to access the remote features
of the product.
EXAMPLE 2 The functions of an internet gateway include forwarding network traffic from private networks to
the internet and vice versa.
EXAMPLE 3 The functions of a network camera include recording optical signals and making those recordings
available via a network.
EXAMPLE 4       Functions that are provided by the product when it is used according to its IPRFU can include
features which ensure the defined security objectives, e.g. certain cybersecurity functions that protect the product,
and the health and safety of the user.
EXAMPLE 5       The ability to configure a product is also a function in the product's IPRFU.

The product's operational environment refers to the external conditions under which it is used within
its IPRFU.
NOTE 1       For any RDPS, the operational environment typically contains information on connectivity, expected
availability, data handled, and any constraints (including third-party platforms).



12

                                                                                             prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



NOTE 2 The product's operational environment significantly influences the likelihood and potential impact of
cybersecurity incidents caused by related vulnerabilities. lt can also include existing measures that mitigate certain
risks. As such, the product's operational environment plays an important role in the identification, assessment,
and appropriate treatment of risks throughout the product lifecycle.
NOTE 3      A description of a product's operational environment can amongst others include:
     the networks where the product is intended and reasonably foreseen to be used, including the networks'
     cybersecurity relevant properties;
     the system into which the product is intended, or can reasonably be foreseen, to be integrated, together with
     other hardware and software components, including the relevant cybersecurity-relevant properties ofthis
     system;
     the physical surrounding of the product, where it is intended and reasonably foreseen to be operated in,
     including its cybersecurity relevant properties.
NOTE 4 Understanding the environment of an RDPS is essential, including where it operates, its network
connections, who its users are, expected uptime, the data it manages, and any limitations.

The product architecture overview includes at least the key components of the product as well as the
product interfaces and dependencies. lt is a high-level overview of the components of a product and its
RDPS.
NOTE 1 Where the product contains RDPS the product architecture overview describes this relation on where
RDPS plays a role in delivering any stated product function. This overview also describes whether the RDPS is
developed by the manufacturer or provided under the manufacturer's responsibility, and who operates it;
NOTE 2 Asystem can contain several components/elements. The physical components/ elements ofthe system
can be placed in different locations, interfacing with a locai network and have an RDPS component.

The product's end user, also referred to in this document as user, is any natural or legal person intended
to install/ operate/handle /use. This can include the use of a product as a component in another product.
The description outlines the user's reasonably foreseeable level of experience, knowledge and ability
to securely install/operate/maintain/decommission the product.

This includes considering if the product is to be used by vulnerable groups of users, far example those
with (temporary or long term) disabilities and/or impairments. Annex D contains more information on
accessible cybersecurity.
NOTE 1 The product user description typically indicates if the user is affected by RDPS dependence and any
expectations placed on users or integrators.
NOTE 2 The product can be intended to be used by users with no training or expertise. In that case it is important
to also account for the use by vulnerable groups of users in determining appropriate controls.
NOTE 3 The product can be intended to be used by a manufacturer as a component in their product. This entails
the expectation of potential mitigation measures put in piace by the user. Communication of these expectations
is a criticai aspect of cybersecurity for components.

The output shall include:
      the product context
      associated evidence (due diligence) in the technical documentati on.

Check whether the product context and the associated evidence in the technical documentation6.2.4 of
the product exists.
Assess whether the product context from 6.2.4 meets the requirements from 6.2.3.
The verdict PASS is assigned if:
      the description of the product context of the product exists;
      there is evidence that the product context meets the requirements.

attributes.clauseTitle: Risk acceptance criteria and risk management methodology

attributes.clauseText:
Establishing the risk acceptance criteria far products is a necessary step to determine whether risk
treatment needs to be applied, whether appropriate risk treatment has been applied, and whether the
residuai risk is acceptable or further mitigation is required.
These criteria are established based on the product's context andare typically determined ahead of the
risk assessment, although they can be adjusted during later stages of development as they are influenced
aver time by changes in the state of the art, the threat landscape, and other relevant factors aver time.
It is important to re-evaluate risk acceptance criteria when necessary.
Some circumstances justify deviating from these criteria far individuai risks. Examples include
situations where the user explicitly accepts certain risks, such as those introduced in tailor made

14

                                                                                           prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



products to ensure compatibility with the customer's environment, or through other contractual
agreements. Communicating the effect on the residuai risk of the product is key.
Risk acceptance criteria will vary far each product context. Additionally, risks can vary depending on
the phase of the product lifecycle and that of its components, such as obsolescence or depreciation.
These criteria can typically be based on a number of common elements such as:
     Regulatory factors. Legislation affecting the product can influence the degree by which a specific
     risk is acceptable. Examples are privacy or other safety legislation.
     Contractual agreements, stakeholder expectations or existing business practices: This
     incorporates a shared risk model. In this the different elements of the supply chain of a product
     are aware ofrisks and take shared responsibility to ensure the risks are mitigated. This can contain
     formai documents indicating shared responsibility.
     The nature of the risks such as:
          The health and safety of the user. Far some products, an exploited vulnerability of the product
          can lead to direct health and safety concerns far the user;
          Discoverability and speed of materialisation of the risk. Some risks can be easily monitored
          and their exploitation detected by users. In other cases the user will not be aware of
          exploitation, or exploitation happens so rapidly that the user is incapable of intervening;
          Attack scalability. The possibility to do attacks of scale with the product, targeting far example
          its RDPS. The quantity of products produced can affect the magnitude of potential loss or
          disruption of an exploited vulnerability in the product if multiple products are exploited
          simultaneously.
     The nature of the product such as:
          Operational environment factors. The operational environment associated with the products'
          IPRFU can have a mitigating or magnifying effect on the product's risk. Far example, if the
          product is used in an environment where external identity and access management is relied
          on, or where other systems protect the network;
          the online hosting location or product related RDPS;
          the number ofproducts on the market.
     The user, the number of impacted users and their capability to mitigate risk further such as:
          Vulnerable users. The product can be used by vulnerable users, requiring additional
          accessibility features or warranting a higher leve I of protection. An example of this is children;
          Professional users. The product can be intended far the use by professionals or in a supervised
          environment, resulting in a greater ability of the user to mitigate risks themselves.
NOTE 1 When multiple Union acts address the same product a risk analysis of the product, or analysis of the
intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable use, is done to determi

The output shall include:
     The product's cybersecurity risks acceptance criteria.
     The applied risk assessment and treatment methodology.

Check whether the risk acceptance crite ria and the applied risk assessment and treatment methodology
of the product exists.
Assess whether the risk acceptance criteria from 6.3.4 meets the requirements from 6.3.3.
Assess whether the applied risk assessment and treatment methodology from 6.3.4 meets the
requirements from 6.3.3.



16

                                                                                            prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



The verdict PASS is assigned if:
     the risk acceptance criteria of the product exists;
     the applied risk assessment and treatment methodology exists;
     there is evidence that the risk acceptance criteria of the product meets the requirements.
     there is evidence that he applied risk assessment and treatment methodology applied to the
     product meets the requirements.

The risk assessment is based on the products' context and the risk assessment results in an evaluation
of identified risks.
The assessment of risks includes:
     an identification of the assets and cybersecurity objectives according to 6.4.2;
     an identification of the threats according to 6.4.3:
     an estimation of the risks according to 6.4.4:
     an evaluation of the risks according to 6.4.5.
NOTE 1       Typically the assets are linked to more high-level objectives related to the product's context.
NOTE 2       Assets in this document refers to assets which are related to, processed by or potentially affected the
product.

NOTE 3 This document does not specify methodologies for a risk analysis. As long as the risk estimation is
based on the likelihood of occurrence or exploitability and the magnitude ofloss or disruption after a successful
attack. Thus, different approaches and models such as the fishbone model, event tree analysis, fault tree models,
attack feasibility ratings or attack potential considerations can be used within the analysis of risks.

The input shall include the product context from 6.2.4.


                                                                                                                 17

prEN 40000-1-2 (E)

Assets shall be identified.
The cybersecurity objectives related to the asset shall be identified.
The output shall include a list ofthe assets and related cybersecurity objectives.

Check whether a list of the assets exists.
Check whether a list of cybersecurity objectives exists.
Assess whether assets and cybersecurity objectives from 6.4.2.4 is complete.
The verdict PASS is assigned if:
     the list of assets exists;
     there is evidence that the list of assets and cybersecurity objectives is complete.

Threat modelling is a security design analysis technique that identifies potential security issues EN IEC
62443-4-1:2018 [3] . Following the assets, it is now possible to determine the threats to the product.
This is to be able to analyse possible risks.
Threat modelling is a structured approach for identifying threats. Threat modelling can consider the
product lifecycle, how a product functions, possible threat actors and/or threat events, and identifies
remaining threats to the product. Examples of threat modelling approaches are frameworks such as
TVRA ETSI TS 102 165-1 [4] . attacktrees .[fil, PASTA .[fil, and STRIDE IZl-
NOTE 1 ThethreatcatalogueTR JT013097:2026 [81 orcomparablesectorspecificthreatcatalogues (e.g. MITRE
fil) can be used as input to determine common threats. lnformation on the product-specific threats can also be
acquired from product-specific European Standards (ENs).
NOTE 2 Threat actors are entities that can intentionally or unintentionally cause harm to the product by
exploiting vulnerabilities. They can include external attackers, insiders such as employees or contractors, or even
unintended users who gain access to the product.

Threats shall be identified and include:
     targeted asset(s);
     compromised cybersecurity objective(s) of the asset(s); and
     cause of compromise of the cybersecurity objective(s).

The output shall include a list containing the threats for each asset.

6.4.3.S    Assessment criteria
Check whether a list of threats exists for each asset.
Assess whether the list of threats for each asset from 6.4.3.4 is sufficient.
The verdict PASS is assigned if:
     a list of the threats for each asset exists;
     there is evidence that the list of threats for each asset is sufficient.

An analysis ofthe likelihood of occurrence and the magnitude ofpotential loss related to the threats is
used to estimate the risks. This is needed to make the risks clearly defined and suitable for comparison
with the risk acceptance criteria.
Different methods can be used to determine and express risk, based on the likelihood of occurrence and
the potential magnitude ofloss or disruption. This can be done in a qualitative or quantitative manner.
NOTE 1 A qualitative estimati on of risks can be performed using risk matrices that map qualitative categories
ofthe likelihood of occurrence and qualitative categories of magni tu de ofpotential loss or disruption to qualitative
risk categories.
NOTE 2 A quantitative estimation of risks can be performed using scoring systems that map qualitative
categories of the likelihood of occurrence and qualitative categories of magnitude of potential loss or disruption
to numerica! values.
NOTE 3 Risk can, amongst others, be expressed in terms of categories of risks, and parameters for estimating
likelihood of occurrence (like attack feasibility) and magnitude ofloss or disruption related to risks.
NOTE 4 Considering the magnitude of potential loss or disruption through damage scenarios can enhance a
risk assessment. This approach helps to better understand potential consequences and to prioritize mitigation
efforts.

The likelihood of occurrence of each threat shall be estimated.


                                                                                                                  19

prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



The magnitude of potential loss or disruption related to the threat shall be estimated.
The risk, based on the likelihood of occurrence and the magnitude of potential loss or disruption, shall
be estimated for each threat.

Check whether the output of 6.4.4.4 exists.
Assess whether the output of 6.4.4.4 aligns the applied risk assessment methodology from 6.3.
The verdict PASS is assigned if:
     output of 6.4.4.4 exists;
     there is evidence thatthe outputof 6.4.4.4 aligns the applied riskassessmentmethodologyfrom 6.3.

Risk evaluation identifies non-acceptable risks requiring treatment and justifies acceptable residuai
risks.

Check whether the output of 6.4.5.4 exists.




20

                                                                                           prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



Assess whether the justification for residuai risk acceptance is aligned with the risk acceptance criteria
from 6.3.
The verdict PASS is assigned if:
      output of 6.4.5.4 exists;
      there is evidence that the justification for residuai risk acceptance is aligned with the risk
      acceptance criteria from 6.3.
The aim of risk treatment is to reduce or mitigate risks so that the residuai risk is acceptable.

Risk avoidance involves choosing not to incorporate certain components in the product, or modifying
the product's context, in arder to avoid the risks related to those choices. This can help avoid some
classes ofvulnerabilities by, for example, using memory-safe programming languages.
Modification of the product context requires risk reassessment.

Notali risks can be avoided. For those that cannot, it is relevant to consider how to mitigate them. Risk
mitigation involves implementing measures that reduce the likelihood of occurrence or magnitude of
potential loss or disruption for a particular threat.
Risk mitigation requires risk reassessment, since mitigation changes existing risks and may introduce
newones.

A risk can be accepted provided it aligns with the predetermined risk acceptance criteria.
For some products, certain risks are inherent and cannot be mitigated or avoided without compromising
function. This is especially relevant and prevalent for products used as components. If these risks are
inherent to the product functions, their existence may be considered acceptable under the risk
acceptance criteria, taking into account the product context. For such risks, it is criticai to communicate
their existence and the measures required to mitigate them when the product is used.
EXAMPLE A component or product lacks access controls due to the nature of its functions. In isolation this
would be an issue, but when used in the intended operational environment appropriate access controls are instead
provided externally. In this case, it is important to clearly communicate that the product is intended to be used in
such an environment, whether physical or digitai.

Any risk remaining after mitigation, even if acceptable, will inherently be non-zero. This residuai risk
does notvanish; it is transferred to the user of the product. Communication is not needed forali residuai
risks, but those inherent to the intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable use are typically the risks
that are to be communicated clearly and in an accessible manner.




                                                                                                                21

prEN 40000-1-2 (E)

The different risk treatment options shall be selected based on the fallowing arder of priority, where
alternatives are listed in decreasing arder of preference:
a)   Risk avoidance.
b)   Risk mitigati on.
e)   Risk acceptance.
d)   Risk transfer.

The input shall include:
     the risk acceptance criteria and risk treatment methodology from 6.3:
     the evaluated risk from 6.4.5.

Far each risk, one or more of the fallowing risk treatment options shall be applied in arder of preference:
     risk avoidance;
     risk mitigation;
     risk acceptance;
     risk transfer.
Risk treatment options with lower priority shall not be selected if appropriate alternatives with higher
priority are available.
After risk mitigation the risks shall be re-evaluated.
Risk acceptance shall only be applied when the risks are acceptable according to 6.4.5 and shall be
documented and justified.
If the risk is acceptable because it is inherent to the product and as such mitigation or avoidance is not
possible without compromising the functions of the product:
     the inherent risk shall be disclosed to the user; and,
     recommended mitigation measures far secure onboarding, integration and operation shall be
     communicated to the user.
Risk transfer shall only be applied when the risks are acceptable according to the evaluation of the risks
and shall be documented and justified.
The output shall include the risk treatment decision with justification per risk.

Check whether the output of 6.5.4 exists.
Assess whether the justification far the risk treatment option is aligned with the risk treatment
methodology from 6.3.



22

                                                                                           prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



The verdict PASS is assigned if:
      output of 6.5.4 exists;
      there is evidence that the justification for the risk treatment option is aligned with the risk
      treatment methodology from 6.3.

Risk communication refers to providing information on risks related to the product based on the product
context
It is necessary to clearly communicate ali relevant risks transferred to the relevant stakeholder, as well
as the actions and measures expected of the stakeholder to mitigate these risks. Where appropriately
this communication considers accessibility aspects (e.g. simple language, multi-modal formats). This
ensures that the stakeholder has the capability to take appropriate actions to mitigate those risks and
securely use the product according to the product context.
NOTE In some cases risk will need to be communicated to more than just the user. This broader category can
be referred to as stakeholders.

The input shall include:
      the threats from 6.4.3.4:
      the risks from 6.4.4.4:
      the risk treatment decisions from 6.5.4.

The communication of relevant risks to affected stakeholders shall be carried out using a method and
terminology that meets the communication needs of each stakeholder.
Where appropriate, the communication with the affected stakeholder shall consider accessibility
aspects (e.g. simple language, multi-modal formats) for each stakeholder.
The communication of the product's risks to affected stakeholders shall include:
      disclosure of residuai risks, e.g. a description of circumstances related to the context that can lead
      to significant cybersecurity risks;
      recommended mitigation measures for the stakeholder, e.g. the environment for onboarding,
      integration and operation;
      relevant assumptions about the product context for onboarding, integration and operation;
      expectations set on end users and downstream integrators.
NOTE 1      Where relevant to the CRA ili this information can be added to the information and instructions to
the user.
NOTE 2 Communication needs depend on the stakeholder. End users can have impairments that prevent them
from accessing this information in written format, or prevents access to the information if it is only available on
a website. When dealing with other manufacturers it can be enough to have the information written in a language
they are able to understand.




                                                                                                               23

prEN 40000-1-2 (E)

The output shall include:
       documentation containing the risk treatment information for the stakeholder;
       documentation containing what is expected from the user, added to the information and
       instructions to the user.

Check whether the output of 6.6.4 exists.
Assess whether the documentation containing the risk treatment information for the stakeholder
contains sufficient information to mitigate the risk.
Assess whether the documentation containing what is expected from the user contains sufficient
information to mitigate the risk.
The verdict PASS is assigned if:
       output of 6.6.4 exists;
       there is evidence that the documentation containing the risk treatment information for the
       stakeholder contains sufficient information to mitigate the risk;
       there is evidence that the documentation containing what is expected from the user contains
       sufficient information to mitigate the risk.

6. 7     Risk monitoring and review
6. 7.1    Generai
It is important to review and, if necessary, up date the elements of risk management to address potential
changes in the threat landscape and state of the art. This review can be triggered by the observation
that the threat landscape has changed or can be done on a regular basis if required.
Review of the risk assessment helps to create awareness of potential cybersecurity issues.
NOTE       Updating relevant parts of the risk management can include adding or modifying product controls.

The input shall include:
       the product context from 6.2.
       the risks acceptance criteria from 6.3.
       the evaluated risks from 6.4.5.
       the risk treatment decision from 6.5.
       risk treatment information for stakeholders from 6.6.

6. 7.3    Requirement
The regularity with which to review the risk management shall be determined based on risk and
justified.
The reviewing of the risk management shall be performed:
       regularly as appropriate to the product's context and implementation;

24

                                                                                    prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



      when the product's cybersecurity risk exposure changes (including changes to the threatlandscape
      and review of the threat model as required);
      when cybersecurity issues occur (e.g. severe incidents, actively exploited vulnerabilities,
      obsolescence of components) that have an impact on the cybersecurity of the product.
The review of the outcome of the risk management shall cover at least the relevant parts of Clause 6.
NOTE This document cannot specify the regularity with which to monitor or review. Context specific
information is needed to specify this information.

6. 7.4    Output
The output shall include:
      at what regularity the reviewing of the risk management shall be performed;
      justification for the regularity with which the reviewing of the risk management shall be performed.
And if the review of the risk management has been triggered it shall contain updates of the relevant
documentation of Clause 6.

6. 7.5 Assessment criteria
Check whether the regularity with which the reviewing of the risk management shall be performed of
6. 7.4 has been determined.
If the review of the risk management has been triggered, check whether updates of the relevant
documentation of Clause 6 exist.
Assess whether the justification for the regularity with which the reviewing of the risk management
shall be performed is reasonable based on the risk.
Assess whether the updates of the relevant documentation of Clause 6 cover the changes needed due
to the trigger of the review.
The verdict PASS is assigned if:
      the regularity with which the reviewing of the risk management shall be performed of 6.7.4 has
      been determined.
      there is evidence that the assessment and justification to determine on what regularity the
      reviewing of the risk management shall be performed is reasonable for the product context and
      implementation.
      when the review has been triggered, that there is evidence that the updates of the relevant
      documentation of Clause 6 cover the changed needed due to the trigger of the review.


7     Cybersecurity activities

Product cybersecurity activities are intended to be process agnostic. There are logical connections
between activities: some are prerequisites for others but, with certain development methodologies
(including agile approaches), the activities in this clause can be executed concurrently or in any order.
Furthermore, many activities can be revisited at relevant points or regular intervals as a change in one
can imply changes in severa} others. In that case, it is necessary to document the dependencies between
process activities.




                                                                                                       25

prEN 40000-1-2 (E)

Cybersecurity planning involves describing the cybersecurity activities for a product throughout its
lifecycle. Relevant activities are found in Clause 6 and Clause 7. Many activities are interrelated. Changes
in one activity can affect others.
NOTE      This type of planning can include considerations on the roles and responsibilities, as well as ensuring
that that personnel are adequately trained, as appropriate for the manufacturer.
The input shall include the output from the activities described in Clause 6 and 7.3 through 7.11.
Documentation containing the requirements in 7.2.3.

Check whether the cybersecurity planning documentation from 7.2.4 exists.
Assess whether the documentation from 7.2.4 meets the requirements of 7.2.3.
The verdict PASS is assigned if:
      the cybersecurity planning documentation exists;
      there is evidence that the documentation meets the requirements.

The product cybersecurity requirements:
      are managed throughout the product lifecycle, in line with the management of cybersecurity risks,
      in particular the assessment and treatment of product cybersecurity risks; and


26

                                                                                         prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



     are based on the needs and expectations of stakeholders relevant to the product, as well as
     regulatory product requirements such as those of the CRA ili-
In additi on, the identification and formulation of product cybersecurity requirements typically consider:
     the traceability, validity, understandability and verifiability of product cybersecurity technical
     specifications;
     the cybersecurity properties of the product's environment during development and production.
These requirements can then be fulfilled through the implementation of specific cybersecurity controls,
typically selected from different catalogues.
NOTE 1     In line with 1SO/IEC terminology, "requirements" in this document can express obligations,
permissions, or prohibitions. They define what is expected. "Controls" (sometimes also referred to as safeguards)
are the measures implemented to fulfil those requirements.
NOTE 2     Examples of catalogues of cybersecurity controls:
     JT013091:2026 [10] (These controls are related to the essential requirements ofthe CRA ill);
     ETSI EN 303 645 [11] ;
     EN IEC 62443-4-2 [12] ;
     EN 1SO/IEC 15408-2:2020 [13] ;
     EN 1SO/IEC 27002:2022 [14] ;
     Guideline "State of the art" in IT security Technical and organisational measures 2025llfil;
     NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Security and Privacy Controls for lnformation Systems and Organizations li.fil.

The product cybersecurity requirements shall be established based on the inputs.
Established cybersecurity requirements shall:
     be documented with respect to their applicability and effectiveness to achieve the cybersecurity
     objectives far the assets;
     have their technical specifications documented;
     have applicable controls selected to fulfil them.



                                                                                                              27

prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



The product cybersecurity requirements shall be reviewed and when necessary updated when there
are changes in any of the listed inputs.
The output shall include documented product cybersecurity requirements.

Check whether documentation specifying the product cybersecurity requirements from 7.3.4 exists.
Assess whether the documentation of the product cybersecurity requirements from 7.3.4 meets the
requirements from 7.3.3.
The verdict PASS is assigned if:
     documentation specifying the product cybersecurity requirements exists;
     there is evidence thatthe documentation meets the requirements specified in 7.3.3.

The secure architecture and the functional design of the product are based on the cybersecurity
requirements as defined in 7.3 and the product context as defined in 6.2.
Consider the fallowing far the product cybersecurity architecture and design:
     introduce trust boundaries between components and subsystems including RDPS, to ensure clear
     separation of privileges and responsibilities, as well as containment;
     secure interface design, with particular attention to authentication, input validation, and
     minimization of the exposed attack surface.

The input shall include:
     product context definition from 6.2.4:
     list of assets and cybersecurity objectives from 6.4.2.4:
     cybersecurity requirements from 7.3.4.

7 .4.3   Requirement
The cybersecurity architecture and design of the product shall be established.
The cybersecurity architecture and design far the product shall consider appropriate elements from:
     the security by design principle from 5.3; and,
     the secure by default principle from 5.4.
The cybersecurity architecture and design shall ensure that third-party component integration is
perfarmed with due diligence, aligned with 7.11 and 7.5.
In case the product contains third-party components or RDPS as identified in the product context, due
diligence shall be applied to ali components, whether third-party or not, and to their integration.




28

                                                                                   prEN 40000-1-2 (E)
The output shall include the documented cybersecurity architecture and design for the product.

Check whether documentation specifying the secure product architecture and design from 7.4.4 exists.
Assess whether the documentation of the secure product architecture and design from 7.4.4. meets the
reguirements from 7.4.3.
The verdict PASS is assigned if:
      the secure product architecture and design documentation exists;
      there is adeguate evidence that the description of the secure product architecture and design meets
      the reguirements on the product's cybersecurity architecture.
      there is adeguate evidence that the cybersecurity architecture and design for the product is
      consistent with the cybersecurity reguirements identified in 7.4.3.

Secure implementation activities ensure the development of secure product that can be tested against
the previously defined cybersecurity reguirements from 7.3. Special considerations for secure
implementation include configuring the cybersecurity properties of components to be integrated into
the product.
Activities of secure implementation can include, but are not limited to:
      Maintenance of the Software Bill of Materials (SBOM). The SBOM lists the components used in the
      software, covering at least the top-level dependencies and relevant parts that gualify it for
      vulnerability monitoring. That entails ali relevant components of an asset or a group of assets.
      Managing dependencies and third-party libraries by selecting secure libraries and keeping them
      up to date. Follow the due diligence in 7.11 when selecting secure libraries;
      Secure code development. Manufacturers often use a set of coding standards and guidelines to
      write secure code. These standards help maintain code guality and consistency, and in avoiding
      common programming errors that could lead to cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Different rules apply
      for different programming languages. Ensure that the rules are appropriate for each programming
      language used. Secure coding practices include using secure functions, prohibiting hard-coded
      credentials, and implementing proper error handling;
      Secure coding and strategies to ensure memory safety, including practices to avoid buffer
      overflows, memory leaks, and other memory-related vulnerabilities. This may involve using safe
      programming languages, employing memory management technigues, and utilizing tools for
      detecting common defects;
      Development of the technical documentation as well as information and instructions for users and
      stakeholders (CRA Annex VII and Ilill).
The secure implementation can result in deviations from the design documentation. Such deviations
can lead to more or less secure behaviour of the product and could impact the se cure architecture, the
functional design, and the cybersecurity risk management activities.




                                                                                                      29

prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



A secure implementation typically relies on a securely maintained development environment that,
amongst other things:
     prevents unauthorized access to components and source materials;
     includes software tools far managing, developing and implementing the software and other
     product-related artefacts;
     manages cryptographic keys and certificates using technology appropriate to their sensitivity.

The input shall include:
     cybersecurity requirements from 7.3.4:
     secure product architecture and design from 7.4.4:
     due diligence of third-party components to be implemented and integrated into the product from
     7.11.

The product shall be developed and maintained in a se cure manner, including through the use of a se cure
development environment.
Secure implementation shall ensure that ali selected cybersecurity controls are correctly implemented
far the product. Secure implementation shall, where appropriate to the design and scope of the product,
include the fallowing activities:
     Preparation and maintenance of an SBOM appropriate far the product;
     Confirmation of the vulnerability status of integrated components and their integrati on, to ensure
     that cybersecurity risks are addressed in the implemented design.
     Use of appropriate technology far the management of cryptographic keys and certificates;
     Preparation of the technical to and infarmation and instructions to the User, made available in an
     accessible manner and in a language easily understood by the user.
NOTE    The cybersecurity of a component and its integration can change at any point throughout the
development cycle and therefore, it is important to verify component cybersecurity at multiple phases.

Check whether the output ofthe secure implementation from 7.5.4 exists.
Assess whether the output from 7.5.4 meets the requirements from 7.5.3.



30

                                                                                     prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



The verdict PASS is assigned if:
      the output of the secure implementation exists;
      there is adeguate evidence that the output of the se cure implementation meets the req uirements.

The goal of cybersecurity verification and validation (V&V) is to ensure that the concept, design and
implementation of a product satisfy ali respective cybersecurity requirements, and that the product is
sufficiently cybersecure considering its context.
V&V is crucial for detecting potential cybersecurity defects (such as coding mistakes, configuration
errors, or design flaws) that could be exploited by malicious actors. Through V&V, the manufacturer
identifies and mitigates or eliminates these vulnerabilities before the product is deployed or released,
thereby reducing the risk of successful cyberattacks.
Cybersecurity V&V focuses on ensuring:
      that the product includes ali intended cybersecurity functions and cybersecurity controls, as
      identified in the cybersecurity requirements from 7.3.4:
      that the implemented cybersecurity controls are effective.
Cybersecurity V&Vis a recurring activity integrated throughout the entire lifecycle, not only at the final
stages. V&V often uncovers implementation issues that can trigger design changes; therefore, these
activities are normally repeated until ali cybersecurity issues are addressed. V&V is also carried out
whenever the product changes, such as during maintenance or after resolution of newly uncovered
vulnerabilities.
For cybersecurity V&V, the testing environment is normally separated from the product's operational
environment lt is a recommended practice to ensure that the testing environment is secure. Where
possible, cybersecurity V&Vis preferred to be carri ed out in an isolated environment
Cybersecurity V&V often includes but are not limited to the following approaches:
      Cybersecurity analysis: a systematic evaluation process in which cybersecurity-related artefacts,
      such as design, specification, user and technical documentation, and code are examined. This can
      include inspections, walkthroughs, V&V reviews etc., undertaken to determine the suitability,
      adequacy, and effectiveness of the subject matter in achieving established cybersecurity objectives.
      Unit testing: focuses on verifying that small, functional units of software behave securely and as
      intended. lt is considered a best practice in software development to implement software as
      testable units and to write corresponding unit tests for each. Unit tests support regressi on testing,
      provide living documentation of expected behaviour, facilitate integration, and encourage good
      design.
      Integration testing: Performed to verify the interaction between different components and identify
      any cybersecurity gaps that can arise:

This annex facuses on enabling manufacturers of consumer cyber products to produce products which
are both secure and accessible to the users.

The EuropeanAccessibility Act (EAA) UQ]_ requires thata wide range of products and services, including
smartphones, ATMs, e-commerce platfarms, and e-readers, are usable by persons with disabilities. This
aligns with the EU's commitment to equal participation in society and the economy, ensuring that no
consumer is excluded from the digitai marketplace.
Security features are often the "front door" to a digitai product. If a consumer cannot navigate
authentication, password recovery, or consent dialogues, they can be left vulnerable-or unable to use
the product at ali. Accessibility in cybersecurity is therefare both a compliance issue under the EAA and
a trust issue far manufacturers who want to serve the widest possible market.
At the same time, the CRA li places obligations on manufacturers to safeguard the users' cybersecurity.
Devices and digitai services are increasingly interconnected, and secure design is essential to protect
consumers from fraud, identity theft, and misuse of persona} data. Therefare it is important that,_
cybersecurity measures themselves are accessible-otherwise they can inadvertently exclude or
disadvantage certain groups of users.
Accessibility and cybersecurity are two sides of the same coin: both protect users, both reduce exclusion,
and both are essential far building a sustainable digitai economy.

Cybersecurity is often designed with the "ideai user" in mind. This ideai user has a limitless memory
and attention to detail, to enable them to be fully aware of system behaviours that indicate suspect
behaviours and the ability to retain and apply ali the rules in organization policies. Very few humans
have ali these abiliti es ali of the time. This is why it is crucial to create a good understanding of what
can be reasonably expected ofthe user demographics, as otherwise many potential users will struggle
and may fail to use the product safely.
When developing cybersecurity solutions, it is required to consider the user abilities and skills needed
to carry out the required interactions with the product. Consumers will be impacted depending on:
      The nature ofthe required interaction.
      The consequence ofthe interaction method on the user's cybersecurity.
      The recommended solution to ensure maximum cybersecurity to the potential users.
Limiting the types of users who can interact with a product will harm people with disabilities and also
people with temporary conditions caused by accident, illness, stress, grief or distraction.




                                                                                                        53

prEN 40000-1-2 (E)

The nature of the required interaction can include (but is not limited to) the following:
      interactions requiring the use of visual or audible information can reduce the cybersecurity for
      blind/visually impaired/colour-blind and/or deaf/hard of hearing people.
      interactions requiring the operation of physical controls can reduce the cybersecurity for people
      with gross or fine control motor control issues, reach issues and/or related issues.
      interactions requiring the understanding of spoken or written information can reduce the
      cybersecurity for people who cannot read or understand a particular language or who have a
      cognitive disability.
      interactions requiring speech control can reduce the cybersecurity for people who are speech
      impaired.

Examples of accessibility issues in cybersecurity requirements include systems which require people
to have specific physical, visual, hearing, memory or cognitive skills. Examples of these are presented
with possible solutions below:
      Systems that time-out too quickly during password entry can disadvantage users who rely on
      assistive technologies such as screen readers or switch devices. Extending the time-out will also
      benefit other users includingthose with physical disabilities or whose attention is limited by stress.
      Biometrie authentication, as facial recognition can fail for users with certain physical disabilities
      or conditions that affect their appearance or ability to stay stili or who are using a system without
      a camera (or fingerprint sensor). Offering multiple authentication methods will enable more
      consumers to authenticate themselves. Ali single method verification methods can cause issues:
           SMS-based codes can be inaccessible to people with hearing loss if voice cali verification is the
           only backup.
           CAPTCHA challenges relying on distorted text or images exclude users with visual loss unless
           multiple, accessible, alternatives (e.g., audio CAPTCHAs or logical puzzles) are provided.
           Fingerprint scanners cannot be usable by individuals with prosthetics or reduced dexterity
           or whose fingerprints are not easily readable due to skin changes caused by age.
           Pop-up alerts that disappear quickly can be inaccessible to users relying on screen readers or
           whose reaction times are reduced by physical factors (temporary by accident or long-term
           physical functional limitation or by slow reactions (caused by stress or cognitive issues or
           distraction by children etc.).
      Cybersecurity updates or recovery processes that depend on a single method of delivery and also
      use unclear terminology will be inaccessible to a range of users.

about the product will enable more users to interact with the product. These changes will not impact
the cybersecurity of the product. User stories can be a valuable input in considering what alternatives
to provide to ensure accessibility to the product.



54

                                                                                   prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



Accessibility requirements and advice can be found in EN 301 549 v3.2.1 "Accessibility requirements
for ICT products and services". Accounting forthese requirements is better done earlier in development
as adding accessibility features can also potentially add vulnerabilities and as such these need to be
accounted for in the risk assessment.


D. 7   Communication with the user
The obligation of the manufacturer to provi de accessibility to the design of the product also extends to
the accessibility of the communication with the user. This is to ensure the user is capable of accessing
the information required for securely installing, operating, maintaining and decommissioning the
product. By conducting heuristic evaluation, cognitive walkthroughs, and accessibilitytesting alongside
cybersecurity testing and design analysis, providing alternative methods of se cure access, and ensuring
compatibility with assistive technologies, manufacturers can not only reduce regulatory risk but also
strengthen consumer trust.

providing manufacturers with a structured foundation far designing and implementing their own
processes. These processes enable manufacturers to manage communication among stakeholders,
proactively discover and collect vulnerability information and reports, and diagnose and remediate
vulnerabilities before they become public, thereby preventing malicious actors from exploiting them.

5.3     [PRE] Preparation

The preparation phase lays the foundation for establishing appropriate vulnerability handling and
disclosure processes and policies to support the subsequent phases, providing a structured,
methodological approach to identify, verify, and address vulnerabilities, including communication. This
phase also includes requirements such as identifying software and hardware components, focusing on
creating the Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), and establishing a coordinated vulnerability disclosure
and vulnerability handling policy.

process and is compatible with the external coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy as per 5.3.3.
The intended audience for the vulnerability handling policy is the internal staff.

5.3.3     [PRE-2] Policy on coordinated vulnerability disclosure

The purpose of the coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy is to communicate the manufacturer's
intentions, responsibilities, and expectations regarding vulnerability disclosure. A coordinated
vulnerability disclosure policy encompasses both two-party coordinati on (e.g. between the reporter
and the manufacturer) and multi-party disclosure involving multiple stakeholders. To support this, the
manufacturer develops and publishes an external coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy and
ensures the related internal activities are in piace to effectively coordinate the disclosure of
vulnerabilities.
In addition, to prevent attackers from gaining early access to sensitive information, reporters typically
notify manufacturers privately, and refrain from public disclosure until a fix is available after an agreed-
upon embargo period has passed. The receipt, verification, and remediation development stages are
generally conducted within this embargo period, ensuring that vulnerabilities are addressed securely
and responsibly by ali the parties involved in the process.

Introduction

Machinery must be safe in order to prevent injuries and loss of life.
The communication with the machine must not lead to hazardous situations.
The manufacturer performs a risk assessment according to EN ISO 12100 to identify all potential hazards.
Vulnerabilities can lead to a corruption of the control system of the machine and hazards can lead to dangerous
situations.
By exploitation of vulnerabilities via communication with the machine, the machine could be operated outside
safe parameters or degrade safety functions.
Vulnerabilities cannot create new hazards.
The probability that someone will use a vulnerability for a malicious attempt cannot be predicted.
The risk can only be assessed in terms of its impact on functional safety.
Vulnerabilities are divided into several types.
This document provides two approaches:
—   Approach A (Clause 5 and 7) has been developed to facilitate compliance for machinery developed without
references to EN IEC 62443 series of standards.

—   Approach B (Clauses 6 and 8) has been provided to facilitate compliance for machinery developed in the
context of the EN IEC 62443-3-3:2019, EN IEC 62443-4-1:2018, EN IEC 62443-4-2:2019.

NOTE 1     The EN IEC 62443 series provides information and a methodology to approach cybersecurity.

This document is intended for use by machinery designers, control system manufacturers and integrators, and
others involved in the specification, design and validation of an SCS.
NOTE 2     See EN IEC 62443-4-1:2018; the manufacturer can be a product supplier or system integrator.

This document does not address the role of the user.

1   Scope

This document provides requirements and recommendations for protection against corruption for machinery,
related products and partly completed machinery referred to in this document as ‘machinery’.
This document provides requirements and recommendations to prevent accidental and intentional (including
malicious) corruption of machines resulting in hazardous situations.
This document applies to:
—   hardware components, including interfaces to remote devices and control systems, that can transmit
signals or data;

—   software and data;

if they could influence the safety of the machinery.
NOTE 1     Topics can overlap with the domain of cybersecurity but are not necessarily identical in their coverage.

NOTE 2     This document does not describe functional sa
attributes.clauseTitle: (informative) Relationship between this European Standard and the essential

attributes.clauseText: Either approach A (Clauses 5 and 7) or approach B (Clauses 6 and 8) shall be applied.

The design and the construction of machinery shall not allow hazardous situations via connections.
A connection (physical, logical and indirect) is any link that can exchange information, for example:
—     a network link,

—     a WIFI connection,

—     a single wire,

—     wires of the power supply,

—     an optical link,

—     a card reader interface,

—     a connection from a machine to external systems:

— building networks

— cloud services

— service tools

NOTE 1       The connectivity can exist through equipment permanently available on site, or equipment temporarily brought
to the location during the installation, operation and maintenance, or decommissioning steps.

NOTE 2       Example of a machinery not to be considered is a simple drilling machine without any possibility of connection.

Following a risk assessment according to EN ISO 12100:2010, where all potential hazards have previously
been identified, the designer shall perform a threat assessment.
The content of the threat assessment can be limited to additional threats that are not covered by the minimum
security measures.
The designer shall define the security context for the machine.
The following principles shall be applied in order to protect a machine from threats that can lead to hazardous
situation(s):
a)    Where vulnerabilities are present, eliminate those that can lead to hazardous situation(s).




      8

                                                                                                           prEN 50742:2025 (E)



EXAMPLE 1        To eliminate any unnecessary interfaces so that the threats cannot exploit this vulnerability.

EXAMPLE 2        JTAG interface(s) used during development and then disabled.

EXAMPLE 3        Elimination can be a result of redesign using different components (maybe from same vendor).

b)    if it is not possible to eliminate vulnerabilities, the designer shall mitigate them.

EXAMPLE          Mitigation, implementation of user authentication on an interface.

c)    For any vulnerabilities that remain after steps a) and b), information for use shall provide all necessary
information for compensating countermeasure by the user. See Annex C.

EXAMPLE            Manufacturer states in the instruction for use that the fieldbus connection of the machine is only designed
for internal(local) connections to another machine in a trusted network and is not allowed to be connected to an untrusted
network.

Vulnerabilities cannot create new hazards, but their exploitation can compromise the protective measures;
therefore, a threat assessment shall be performed.
NOTE       By exploitation of vulnerabilities via communication with the machine, the machine could be operated outside
safe parameters or degrade safety functions. The risk can only be assessed in terms of its impact on functional safety.

Countermeasures shall not negatively affect the functional safety of the machinery.
EXAMPLE           When a cryptographic function is implemented, it needs to be verified that it does not lead to hazardous
situations due to increased safety function response time.

The probability that someone will try to exploit a specific vulnerability for a malicious attempt cannot be predicted.
Therefore, the likelihood of being a target/victim shall not be relevant for the threat assessment.
In order to fulfil the essential requirements and recommendations to prevent accidental and intentional (including
malicious) corruption of machines resulting in hazardous situations, designers shall follow approach A in below
table.
However,   if   designers     prefer     to   follow   EN IEC 62443-3-3:2019,         EN IEC 62443-4-1:2018,
EN IEC 62443-4-2:2019 for the security requirements for their machinery, they shall follow approach B.
Table 1 provides an overview of both approaches:
Table 1 — Process requirements overview

           — Risk assessment according to EN ISO 12100:2010
           — Clause 4 - Protection against corruption
           — Clause 9 - Information for use

                               Approach A                                                   Approach B
           — Clause 5 for process requirements                         — Clause 6 for process requirements
           — Clause 7 for product requirements                         — Clause 8 for product requirements

NOTE        Both routes are equally allowed to be followed. The selected route depends to the effort the manufacturer needs
to do, as well as the value for the manufacturer, but also their knowledge, field of application, ect.

7     Product requirements

All machinery interfaces that are accessible and can affect the safety of the machinery shall be identified and
protected using countermeasures or compensating countermeasures.
Figure 2 shows an example of machinery interfaces which can be subject to an attack.




263

Figure 2 — Machinery interfaces example

Guidelines on second order attack are in Annex C.

Security measures to protect against corruption of the machinery leading to hazardous situations shall be
selected on a risk-based approach in order to be adequate.
This risk-based approach shall consider both safety risks and threat risks of the machinery's intended use and
security context.
Security measures shall not negatively affect the functional safety.

Where cryptographic methods are used, only state of the art algorithm should be selected.
NOTE 1    Information related to state-of-the-art algorithms is available from organizations such as ENISA
www.enisa.europa.eu. A list of examples is available in the bibliography [2][3][4].

NOTE 2      When a cryptographic function is implemented, it can be verified that it does not lead to hazardous situations
due to increased safety function response time.




                                                                                                                             11

      prEN 50742:2025 (E)

The following list provides types of interventions that shall be considered:
a.    safety parametrization/configuration parameters (via identification means like CRC…),

EXAMPLE connecting or disconnecting flash drive or SD card, when being used for storing configuration data and
logging data that is relevant for compliance of machinery

b.    SRESW update/modification (via identification means only, such as version number, CRC, ect…),

c.    SRASW updates/modification (via identification means only, such as version number, CRC, ect…),

d.    parametrization of human-machine interfaces if it can creates hazards,

e.    software relevant for displaying safety instructions.

NOTE 1      Any intervention that does not result in changes of the data listed above does not need to be logged (e.g.
successful/unsuccessful authorized interventions).

NOTE 2       Actions on the machine triggering a safe state of the machine e.g. triggering safety light curtain, are not in scope.

NOTE 3       The version of the SRASW binaries or SRESW binaries does not need to be kept in the tracing log.

Digital evidence of a legitimate or illegitimate action or event that changes or interrupts the behaviour, state or
operation of the machinery temporarily or permanently, that changes the software or data shall be recorded and
shall contain the following data as a minimum:
a.    an indication of the type of intervention that affects software relied on for risk reduction according to the risk
assessment,

b.    means to allow correlation of logged events, (e.g. timestamping referring to absolute or relative system
time), boot counts, system times, running counters,

c.    deletion of the log file.

NOTE         Timestamping can be provided by the device making the log event or the remote log collector.

The machine shall provide digital or physical means for traceability related to interventions.
Digital evidence of interventions shall be readable and accessible.
The documentation shall provide information on how to access and interpret the recorded evidence.
If a binary format is used, the format should be documented as part of the information for use, so that anyone
can program a converter to make the logs intelligible.
Where collection of digital evidence is not reasonably practicable, physical evidence (e.g. tampering of a seal)
shall be used.
Evidence collection of interventions is required and shall be done automatically by the machinery or related
product.
NOTE         See Annex A for examples of recognized industry practice on logging standards.




      12

                                                                                                       prEN 50742:2025 (E)



The log records may be stored in the control system, the components inside the machine or in a component for
storing the data external to the machinery (e.g. Network Attached Storage (NAS), local hard drive, etc…).

Log storage shall contain, as a minimum, the evidence of the last intervention of each type.
Tracing log data records of each intervention shall be stored for at least five years.
The tracing log shall be enabled, as a minimum, from the time the machine is put into service.

Logs shall be properly secured to protect against tampering.
Log deletion, if applicable, shall only be possible by an authorized procedure.

Corruption can compromise the integrity and effectiveness of the risk-reduction measures, leading to potentially
hazardous consequences.
To safeguard against such risks, it is essential to first determine the required level of protection.
This involves identifying the vulnerabilities and specific needs of the application in question and defining Safety-
related Security levels (SRSL) for the individual risk-reduction measures.
Once the appropriate level of protection is identified, adequate measures can be applied to mitigate the threats
effectively.
These measures are intended to preserve the integrity and reliability of the safety control system.

For each identified safety function, a Safety-related security level (SRSL) shall be determined and documented.
The determination of the SRSL shall be based on the result of the threat assessment and shall correlate to the
risk-reduction applied by the protective measure and to the likelihood of a successful threat exploitation.
Four SRSL levels are defined, where SRSL0 gives no specific additional requirements, and SRSL1 to SRSL3
correspond from low to high security levels.
NOTE       Annex B provides guidance for the determination of the SRSL. The likelihood of a successful threat exploitation
can be expressed as an attack potential (AP) being a function of several parameters such as Attacker Capability (AC),
Window of Opportunity (WoO) and Exposure Level (EL).

The measures associated with an appropriate Safety Related Security Level (SRSL) shall be selected to protect
safety functions.
Table 2 — SRSL description

       SRSL          Description
       SRSL0         This level shall be used for completely isolated safety system.
                     (e.g. completely isolated networks within the machine; or where safety functions have no
                     external interfaces.)
       SRSL1         This level (or higher) shall be selected to protect safety functions when the attack potential is
                     low, where an attack can only occur under very specific circumstances. When the severity of
                     the harm is reversible, it might also be selected for a moderate attack potential where an
                     attack has a reasonable likelihood of occurring.
       SRSL2         This level (or higher) shall be selected to protect safety functions when the attack potential is
                     moderate, where an attack has a reasonable likelihood of occurring. When the severity of the



                                                                                                                             13

      prEN 50742:2025 (E)




       SRSL          Description
                     harm is reversible, it might also be selected for a significant attack potential where an attack
                     has a high likelihood of occurring.
       SRSL3         This level (or higher) shall be selected to protect safety functions when the attack potential is
                     significant or critical, where an attack has a high likelihood of occurring or an attack is almost
                     guaranteed to occur.
                     This can be used for connection to untrusted networks e.g. connection to internet.

The machinery shall meet, as a minimum, the security protection requirements listed below corresponding to
the determined SRSL.
The security protection requirements shall apply to their respective safety functions and their related interfaces.
NOTE        Interface can be “logical interfaces” (Modbus/TCP, Webserver….) on “physical interfaces” (RJ45, USB).

SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
Entities shall be authenticated.
SRSL2:
Entities shall be authenticated.
SRSL3:
Entities shall be uniquely authenticated.
NOTE 1      In this context the word “entities” relates to human users, software processes, device capable of intervention.

NOTE 2      Authentication means include but are not limited to: passwords/ PIN/ dongle/ biometrics/ certificates/ RFID/
NFC/ logical identifiers (e.g. UID, HID, cookies, etc…) or via cryptographic authentication mechanisms such as random
challenge, TLS-handshake, X509 certificate, etc ….

SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
Interventions shall require authorization.
SRSL2:
Interventions shall require authorization.
SRSL3:
Interventions shall require authorization with specific privileges (e.g. role-based access control).

SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
The integrity of software and other critical information such as safety-related configurations, shall be verified at
startup (e.g. by use of checksums).
SRSL2:
The integrity of software and other critical information, such as safety-related configurations, shall be verified at
startup and periodically (e.g. by use of checksums).
SRSL3:
The integrity of software and other critical information shall be cryptographically verified at startup and
periodically during operation (e.g. by use of cryptographic hashes, HMACs, CMACs).

SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
Integrity of the boot process shall be protected and shall be verified at startup (e.g. checksums).
SRSL2:
Integrity of the boot process shall be protected and shall be verified at startup.
SRSL3:
A secure boot process shall be implemented (e.g. cryptographic signature verification with trusted roots, rollback
or safe state upon verification failure).

SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
The integrity of exchanged information shall be verified.
SRSL2:
The integrity of exchanged information shall be verified.
SRSL3:
The integrity of exchanged information shall be guaranteed by implementing secure cryptographic protocols
that detect and reject modified or replayed messages.

SRSL0:
None
SRSL1:
Input data shall be validated against defined boundaries.



                                                                                                                        15

      prEN 50742:2025 (E)



Invalid input data shall be rejected.
SRSL2:
Input data shall be validated rigorously, including syntax, semantics, format correctness, and data-type
verification.
Invalid input data shall be rejected.
SRSL3:
Input data shall be validated rigorously using strict, context-aware validation including syntactical, semantic,
boundary, and protocol-specific constraints.
Invalid input data shall be rejected.

SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
Physical tampering shall be detected e.g. seal breaking.
SRSL2:
Physical tampering shall be detected e.g. seal breaking.
SRSL3:
Physical tampering shall be detected e.g. seal breaking.

SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
None.
SRSL2:
The authenticity of critical data (e.g. SRESW/SRASW, and critical configuration data) shall be verified via e.g.
cryptographic signatures or equivalent at installation time.
SRSL3:
The authenticity of critical data (e.g. SRESW/SRASW, and critical configuration data) shall be verified via
cryptographic signatures or equivalent at installation time.

Identification of software versions and configuration information relevant for protection against corruption shall
be available on demand. Software identification and configuration information shall be available in human
readable form, either by a built-in system or by an external tool.
NOTE 1       A laptop or a mobile phone with a readily available application can be considered as an example of a commonly
available tool.

NOTE 2      Distinction needed for machinery identification and related products identification through system (HW).

Machinery components shall comply with EN IEC 62443-4-2:2019, 4.2 support of essential functions (CCSC 1)
and 4.4 least privilege (CCSC 3).
Compensating countermeasures implemented in the machinery system may be taken into account for achieving
the security requirements of machinery components as per EN IEC 62443-4-2:2019, 4.3 (CCSC2). A machinery
component may have a lower SL-C than required in Table 4 if this machinery component is part of a machinery

Identification of software versions and configuration information relevant for safety functions shall be available
on demand. Software identification and configuration information shall be available in human readable form,
either by a built-in system or by an external tool.
NOTE        Typical external tools include laptop, portable device or a mobile phone with a readily available application.

Audit records as per EN IEC 62443-4-2:2019, 6.10 (CR 2.8 – Auditable events) shall be persistent for at least
5 years.

Information for use shall include:
—     information about the security context for the machine,

—     identification of software versions and configuration information relevant for safety function,

—     instruction on how to access the information about the software versions and configuration relevant to
safety functions and changes to them,

—     information about permission and/or prohibition of modifications.

Examples of logging formats


This is an informative annex to provide the reader of the standard further information relating to logging formats.
It is however not necessary to follow these examples in order to meet the essential requirements outlined in this
document
CLF - Common Log Format: The Common Log Format is a file format that is used for logging web server
requests.
NOTE 1     See also RFC 6872; examples can be found here: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6872

Syslog: Syslog is a protocol for recording and transmitting log messages common on a wide range of systems.
Many types of network devices, IoT systems, desktops, and servers support the protocol and its standard
plaintext format makes messages easy for machines and humans to read.
NOTE 2     See also RFC 5424.

W3C extended Log File Format: the extended log file format is designed to meet the following needs:
—   permit control over the data recorded,

—   support needs of proxies, clients and servers in a common format,

—   provide robust handling of character escaping issues,

—   allow exchange of demographic data,

—   allow summary data to be expressed.

The log file format described permits customized logfiles to be recorded in a format readable by generic
analysis tools.

NOTE 3     Examples can be found here: https://www.w3.org/TR/WD-logfile

CEF - Common Event Format: The Common Event Format (CEF) is an industry standard format used in
conjunction with syslog messages by many security vendors to enable interoperability of events between
different platforms
The Common Event Format (CEF) is a standardized logging format developed by ArcSight (now part of Micro
Focus), a security information and event management (SIEM) solution provider. CEF is designed to simplify the
process of logging security-related events and making it easier to integrate logs from different sources into a
single system. CEF is based on the syslog format, which is a standard for message logging that is supported
by most network devices and operating systems.
BSI minimum standard for the logging and detection of cyber attacks: With this minimum standard, the BSI
defines a uniform approach to the detection of cyber attacks as required by the 2017 Implementation Plan while
establishing a basis for the specification and implementation of organizational and technical measures.

Threat assessment


To objectively determine the adequate and appropriate requirements, the first steps are to do define Assets,
Define Security Context, Trust Boundaries and model the system (e.g. by using a dataflow diagram), for example
as described in the relevant parts of Annex C.
The safety-related security level (SRSL) is the key property to decide on the appropriateness and adequacy of
protective measures. The level also determines which malicious attempts are reasonably foreseeable and must
be guarded against.
The first parameter to define is the Exposure Level (EL), which is proportionate to the attack surface of the
interface and connection under consideration.
An effective strategy to reduce the exposure level of safety functions is to perform network segregation between
safety relevant and non-safety relevant network parts.
All connections to safety functions need to be evaluated.
If a connection crosses Trust Boundaries (C.6), its exposure level is the higher one. E.G. a connection between
EL1 and EL2 will be considered as EL2.
NOTE        Further network segmentation inside each EL level are permitted.

— This simple machine does not include any web-based interfaces

For the purpose of this example the safety function is used from EN 415-3:2021, 4.3.10 (vertical form, fill
and seal machine):

— Stopping sealing, perforating and cutting mechanisms when the interlocking guard is opened.

— Preventing unexpected start-up of sealing, perforating and cutting mechanisms when the interlocking
guard is open.

— Disconnecting and dissipating energy from the static eliminator when the interlocking guard is opened.

— Stopping the sealing, perforating and cutting mechanisms when the discharge conveyor is not in place.

— Stopping the packaging material transport mechanism when the interlocking guard is opened.

— Stopping the discharge conveyor when the interlocking guard is opened.

— Stopping all hazardous processes by the emergency stop circuit.

The outcome of an analysis will point out a list of components (assets) that have an implication on safety. (see
1.b of Figure 1).
This list can include assets such as interlocks, pressure meters, temperature sensors, motion controllers.
NOTE        Consider the assets for all use cases in all life cycle phases, such as commissioning, normal operation, disposal,
etc. (see Table B.3 of EN ISO 12100:2010).

In this example the safety related assets are identified as:
—    safety configuration data,

—    safety-related application software,



                                                                                                                                 31

      prEN 50742:2025 (E)



—    configuration memory devices (e.g. SD card in s-PLC),

—    safety-related embedded software (Firmware in safety devices),

—    process data on safety related connections (e.g safety buses, safety wireless …),

—    switch to activate engineering mode that allows output simulation etc.,

—    safety functions intended as mitigation defined for a particular hazard of the machine.

In this example the safety related assets are identified as:
—    The safety related data exchanged between controller and receiver

NOTE       EN 62745, 4.3 requires measures against random corruption.

—    Access to the remote controller

NOTE       EN 62745, 4.2.2 requires this as well.
